item.title: Why a New European Security Architecture Will Be Born Through War
item.description: Prof. Glenn Diesen
item.dc:creator: Glenn Diesen
item.content:encoded:
As the world has shifted from unipolarity to multipolarity, the security architecture must also change to ensure peace. From Europe to the Middle East and East Asia, existing security architectures are collapsing, and new arrangements are needed to prevent great-power wars that could destroy humanity. The problem is that new security architectures have historically been established only after major wars that have shattered the previous status quo.

War as the Catalyst for Change

After the Napoleonic Wars, the Concert of Europe was established and organised relations from 1815 to 1914. After the First World War, a new security architecture was developed with the League of Nations, yet it collapsed in 1939 with the outbreak of the Second World War. After the Second World War, the United Nations was established to manage relations and develop shared international law. Yet, throughout the Cold War, we had a dual system, as the international system was organised under the UN, while the bipolar international distribution of power organised competing alliance systems under NATO and the Warsaw Pact.

When the Cold War came to an end, the dual system continued to exist. The West initially signed agreements for a new, inclusive pan-European security architecture based on indivisible security and without dividing lines, as outlined in the Charter of Paris for a New Europe in 1990 and the establishment of the Organisation for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) in 1995 – both based on the Helsinki Accords of 1975. Yet, these agreements were hollowed out by expanding NATO as an instrument of hegemonic peace, creating a new Europe without Russia as the largest country in Europe. The redivision of Europe and the undermining of the principle of indivisible security have been at the heart of the conflict between NATO and Russia for the past three decades, and this was the trigger for the Ukraine War.

New security architectures are historically born through war, as the former status quo disappears and there is a recognition of the need to establish a system to avoid war and build peace. Institutions are usually effective and problem-solving in their early phases, as their objectives are clear. In the later stages, they become decadent and institutionalised, consumed by bureaucracy and institutional self-preservation, while resisting adaptation to new realities. NATO’s transformation is an interesting example of an effort at institutional adaptation and self-preservation, as open debates focused on finding a new purpose for the military bloc that had lost its Soviet adversary – with the slogan for embracing internationalism and expansionism being “out of area or out of business”.

Europe Searching for a Role in the Multipolar World

All the major actors are finding new roles in the multipolar world. China and Russia are taking the lead in establishing a new geoeconomic architecture and political institutions such as BRICS and the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation to facilitate a greater role for rising powers in the multipolar world. The US seeks to preserve or revive its former hegemonic position, yet is reluctantly adjusting to new realities by shifting its focus to the Western Hemisphere and East Asia.

The Europeans are the most reluctant to adjust to new realities, as their former role as the principal partner of the US in an international system defined by collective hegemony ensured Europe’s unity and relevance. There is also a lack of options in terms of what Europe can transition towards, as the US provided Europe with an economic model, security model, and political model, and was indeed the pacifier that ensured unity on the continent over the past decades. The Europeans can throw their full weight behind the US and face vassalage, although the failure to diversify their ties will only weaken Europe further, while a retreating US will see Europe as increasingly less relevant in the new world. Alternatively, Europe must adjust to a new international distribution of power and find unity through a geoeconomic logic of collective bargaining power and the pursuit of collective technological sovereignty. Yet, a geoeconomic Europe must adjust to realities and seek connectivity with the other centres of power – which includes Russia.

This will not happen. The institutions of the former status quo, such as NATO, are still present, which keeps alive the hope of returning to the unipolar order. On 6 November 2026, the EU foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, made this argument explicitly as she dismissed Russia’s call for reforming the European security architecture, stating: “We already have European security architecture in place. NATO and the European Union both have their respective roles. We must make sure Ukraine is integrated into this architecture.” German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul similarly argued: “Europe does not need a new security architecture, as Russia wants us to believe, but rather the simple restoration of the existing security architecture”. The massive war in Europe, which could quickly spiral into nuclear war, did not seem to affect their assessment of the stability of the former status quo.

War is Coming

As history has demonstrated, former security architectures remain in place long after they have outlived their function and decadence has set in. In an act of desperation and self-delusion, the Europeans embrace absurd narratives of being confronted with another Hitler to reinvent a purpose for the outdated and decadent security architecture that no longer provides security. Unwilling to accept new realities and discuss a new European security architecture, the Europeans will choose war as their Ukrainian proxy army collapses on the battlefield. Any pathway to peace that entail recognising the security concerns of Russia has been rejected as it will undermine the former hegemonic security architecture. As in the past, a new security architecture will be built after the coming war between Europe and Russia – if we survive it.

item.title: The Fragmenting West & Europe’s Failure to Adjust to a Multipolar World
item.description: The bipolar world during the Cold War and unipolar world after the Cold War created distinctive conditions that preserved the internal cohesion of the political West.
item.dc:creator: Glenn Diesen
item.content:encoded:
The bipolar world during the Cold War and unipolar world after the Cold War created distinctive conditions that preserved the internal cohesion of the political West. However, in the current multipolar order, the West will predictably continue to fragment, and Europe will unleash a crisis in the international system due to its failure to adjust.

The Cold War & Post-Cold War Era

The world order defined by transatlantic unity was formed by the unique outcome of the Second World War. The world had two centres of power, and the political West based its unity on balancing the Soviet bloc. The bipolar distribution of power was also supported by two competing ideologies that defined the differences between the in-group ‘us’ and the out-group ‘them’. Economic rivalry within the Western bloc was tempered by the need for cohesion, as military rivalry with the Soviet bloc took priority.

After the Cold War, there was only one centre of power in the world: the United States. Western solidarity during the unipolar era was based on the principle of collective hegemony in Europe, which manifested itself in NATO expansion, as opposed to pursuing an inclusive pan-European security architecture in accordance with the Charter of Paris for a New Europe (1990) that also accommodated Russian security interests. The US required Europe as a key partner and node to ensure global primacy, while the Europeans aspired to collective hegemony based on two equal pillars – the US and the EU. The objectives and expectations for the unipolar moment did not fully harmonise, as is evident from the Wolfowitz Doctrine, based on the Defense Planning Guidance from February 1992, in which the US even considered the rise of Germany a threat to US primacy. Yet, the contradictions between the US desire for global primacy and the European approach to collective hegemony were managed.

The shared ideology of the unipolar moment was ‘liberal hegemony’, in which the dominance of the West would supposedly benefit all of humankind by elevating the role of democracy and human rights. The aspiration for hegemony is predictably supported by the claim of representing universal values, as this lays the foundation for a world order based on sovereign inequality. Democracy promotion, humanitarian interventionism, and other post-Cold War policies had the common denominator of promoting sovereignty for the liberal democratic in-group ‘us’, but limited sovereignty for the out-group ‘them’.

The Inevitable and Chaotic End of Hegemony

The unipolar moment was predictably transitional and would eventually come to a disorderly end. Hegemons exhaust their resources as resource are diverted from the core to the periphery, and encourage rising powers to collectively balance the dominant power.

The political West is now trapped with unsustainable debt and an excessively financialised economy, and it is increasingly balanced by the BRICS nations seeking a multipolar distribution of power and a world that elevates civilisational distinctiveness above universal values. The political legitimacy of ‘liberal hegemony’ is also exhausted, as the pretence of supporting equality, self-determination and democracy contradicts the hegemonic structures and sovereign inequality. For three decades, the world has learned that whenever the West spoke of liberal democratic values, it was loading bombs onto planes in the pursuit of strategic interests.

The hegemonic hangover undermines the ability of the West to adjust to a multipolar world. Strategic thinking declines as a hegemon seeks to be everywhere and, thus, fails to prioritise. A hegemon is under the constant lure of imposing its will through military force, and warmongers on both the left and right predictably rise to the top. A hegemon can absorb a lot of costs and can thus make many costly mistakes. A hegemon forgets about diplomacy as mutual understanding and compromise are replaced with ultimatums and threats. Peace for a benign hegemon is achieved by defeating rivals and with good values overwhelming evil, not by managing security competition under a balance of power. Empathy for the security of adversarial countries diminishes as a hegemon considers itself benign and a force for good, which implies that dissent is illegitimate and dangerous. The incompetent political leadership across the West is thus partly the legacy of ‘liberal hegemony’.

The Multipolar World & Fragmentation of the West

The multipolar distribution of power is already a reality. Whether or not people think it is a good thing is irrelevant, yet the costs of ignoring reality are immense. The US will need to start prioritising, and it will prioritise the Western Hemisphere as its own backyard and East Asia, where its peer competitor China is positioned – Europe is, for the first time, a distant third. A formidable US presence in Europe consumes too many of its resources and threatens Russia, which will then pivot excessively towards China. The former US hegemon will see an interest in pulling back to restore its strength and allow the other great powers to instead balance each other.

The US will have to adjust to the new international distribution of power and these new realities, or it will be compelled to do so. The US could attempt to be everywhere at the same time, but by prioritising everything, it would prioritise nothing. Case in point, the US sent its interceptor missiles to fight the proxy war against Russia, which left it with too few interceptor missiles to fight Iran. To make up for the shortage of interceptor missiles in the war against Iran, the US then diverted missiles from Europe and East Asia to the Middle East. Consequently, East Asian allies now recognise the vulnerability of being frontline states of a declining hegemon, and the Europeans will slowly come to the same realisation. The Gulf states are also reaching this conclusion, as Israel took priority in terms of the interceptor missiles that were sent to the Middle East. Subsequently, the US can either scale back its empire in an organised manner and set priorities, or see a disorganised collapse.

As US and European security interests diverge, we will see NATO decline and likely die. NATO expansionism was a manifestation of the unipolar world order, as the political West established collective hegemony by reviving the dividing lines in Europe and gradually pushing them east towards Russian borders. Making an enemy out of Russia was the price the Americans and Europeans paid for the transatlantic partnership and collective hegemony in Europe. NATO expansion to Ukraine was a bridge too far, which has now been balanced by Russia. In the Middle East and East Asia, the US has been balanced by Iran and China. The initial assumption in Europe was that the new war with Russia would recommit the US to Europe, although defeat has instead intensified the US departure.

The reason why most small and medium-sized countries welcome the multipolar world is their ability to diversify economic connectivity and strategic partnerships, which elevates their strategic autonomy as they are not beholden to any one state. The systemic incentive for the Europeans is therefore also to diversify by connecting with Russia, China, India and other great powers. Europe is thus at a crossroad. The political leadership still aspires to revive a collective hegemony that is already gone, yet it results in hostile policies that sever ties with China, Russia and other rivals of the US – yet the Europeans then discover that they will not be rewarded but instead become vulnerable vassals due to excessive dependence on the US. An autonomous Europe also cannot build its unity on having Russia as a common enemy, as Europe will not have economic prosperity or security without working relations with Russia. In short geopolitical Europe destroys geoeconomic Europe.

The European leaders who insist on continued war with Russia are collapsing in the opinion polls. New leaders will thus emerge who will question why the European continent is being redivided and the Cold War logic revived when unipolarity is over and the US is departing. New European leaders, especially in Germany, will recognise that peace and prosperity demand friendly relations with Russia. Furthermore, removing Ukraine from the frontlines of a divided continent will also save that nation from destruction. However, the current political leadership will then be exposed for having deceived its own public – after all, if this war was a conflict over the European security architecture, why did European leaders boycott diplomacy for years as hundreds of thousands of young men died, European economies fell apart, and we took new steps towards nuclear war? The current political leadership will thus attempt to hold on to power and keep the war going, and in the process threaten to unleash a crisis of political legitimacy at home and another world war.

item.title: When Reporting on Ukrainian Victims Becomes "Russian Propaganda"
item.description: Prof. Glenn Diesen
item.dc:creator: Glenn Diesen
item.content:encoded:
This article outlines the little we know about the abuse of the Ukrainian soldiers detained near Kiev, and also why we know so little: the media’s whitewashing of the story and the wider problem of how NATO has used Ukrainian nationalists as a veto power to perpetuate a forever war. The argument being made is that the popular will and suffering of Ukrainians is denounced as “Russian propaganda” if it undermines the narratives required to continue the war.

The Event

On November 2, 2026, violent clashes erupted outside a Ukrainian National Guard facility in Petropavlivska Borshchahivka, near Kiev, following allegations that people were being unlawfully detained and tortured inside. Those detained were reportedly mobilized Ukrainian soldiers and deserters, who emerged from the facility with injuries.

The most dramatic video to emerge from the event showed a 14-year-old boy seemingly in shock as he was escorted out of the building. The boy had not been detained with the other men but had been one of the protesters who climbed on top of a wall. In an interview, the boy said that the soldiers operating the facility threw bricks at him and hit him with shovels, causing him to fall inside. Thereafter, he was pulled into the building for an unknown period of time, during which he was kicked, punched, and struck with shovels, while his clothes were cut with knives.

The facility was being run by Azov, a well-documented neo-Nazi unit that has since been integrated into Ukraine’s National Guard. Its insignia draws on symbols associated with Nazi Germany during the Second World War, such as the Wolfsangel and the Black Sun. The founder of Azov and head of National Corps is Andriy Biletsky, who had earlier declared his vision for Ukraine: “The historic mission of our nation in this critical moment is to lead the White Races of the world in a final crusade for their survival. A crusade against the Semite-led Untermenschen”.[1]

Human rights organisations have for years reported on the torture taking place in Ukraine, although with very little interest from the media. Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch, and the UN have written many reports about torture in Ukraine and Russia in the past:

  • “Ukraine: Abuses and war crimes by the Aidar Volunteer Battalion in the north Luhansk region” (2014).[2]

  • “Ukraine: Breaking Bodies: Torture and Summary Killings in Eastern Ukraine” (2015).[3]

  • “Ukraine: Torture and Secret Detention on Both Sides of the Conflict Line” (2016).[4]

  • “You Don’t Exist”: Arbitrary Detentions, Enforced Disappearances, and Torture in Eastern Ukraine (2016).[5]

  • Joint Statement on Detention-Related Abuses in the Armed Conflict in Ukraine (2017).[6]

  • “Ukraine: Justice Needed for Former Secret Prison Detainees” (2018).[7]

  • “Arbitrary detention, torture and ill-treatment in the context of armed conflict in eastern Ukraine, 2014-2021” (2021).[8]

  • “Treatment of Prisoners of War and Persons Hors de Combat” (2023).[9]

  • “Treatment of Prisoners of War and Update on the Human Rights Situation in Ukraine” (2024).[10]

There are endless videos of the ruthless conscription and “busification” of Ukrainian men on Ukrainian Telegram channels, and this brutal every-day reality is known by every Ukrainian in the country. However, the Western media has demonstrated little if any interest.

The Media Whitewashing: A “Pro-Ukrainian” Narrative Above the Truth

Western media coverage has been almost absent, and the little attention devoted to the matter has been aimed at whitewashing the incident and muddying the waters. The event is portrayed as a Russian disinformation campaign, with the focus on the boy’s participation in the protests being used to suggest that the entire event was staged. The Russian media jumped on the story for the same reason that the Western media ignored it: it discredits the authorities in Kiev. If something like this had happened in Russia, the situation would likely be reversed, with endless Western media coverage.

To turn the entire incident into a non-event, the recurring word used to dismiss the story is “unverified”, with reference to the beatings and torture. However, how can anything be verified in the current propaganda war? Will the Ukrainian authorities investigate themselves, or will Western media pursue any investigative journalism against their proxy army? Of course not. Any journalist who reported objectively would certainly be accused of supporting “Russian narratives”, and their career would be over. That is what journalism has been reduced to: a war of narratives to mobilise public support for war. The pursuit of truth is long gone. Thus, the predictable response from the media was to either ignore or whitewash.

NATO war propaganda dismisses any criticism of Zelensky as “anti-Ukrainian” and “pro-Russian propaganda”. Why? These are crimes committed against Ukrainians. However, this has been a consistent feature of the proxy war: ignoring the will and suffering of Ukrainians under the banner of “standing with Ukraine” against Russia.

Between 1991 and 2014, only approximately 20% of Ukrainians wanted NATO membership, yet they were pulled into NATO’s orbit as a “pro-Ukrainian” policy. In 2014, the toppling of President Yanukovych did not have majority support in Ukraine, yet NATO countries backed it as “standing with Ukraine”. Thereafter, Ukrainian opposition parties, media, culture, language rights, and the Orthodox Church have been purged with the eager support of the West, under the guise of liberating Ukrainians from Russia. These are Ukrainians whose rights have been taken away from them, yet anyone standing up for them would be smeared as supporting “Russian propaganda”. The Minsk peace agreement was sabotaged for seven years, the election outcome in 2019 was subverted, and the Istanbul agreement of 2022 was torpedoed under the claim of helping Ukraine avoid “capitulation”, irrespective of what Ukrainians wanted.

No Western journalists thought it was newsworthy that both the Turkish and Israeli mediators in Istanbul confirmed that the Ukrainians and Russians were close to a peace based on restoring Ukrainian neutrality, before the US and UK intervened as they saw an opportunity to weaken Russia by prolonging the war. Even Zelensky had stated in late March 2022, during an interview with the Economist: “There are those in the West who don’t mind a long war because it would mean exhausting Russia, even if this means the demise of Ukraine and comes at the cost of Ukrainian lives”.[11] Around the same time, in late March 2022, Niall Ferguson reported in Bloomberg that sources in the US and UK governments confirmed that the desire was for “the conflict to be extended and thereby bleed Putin”, as “the only end game now is the end of Putin regime”. No Western journalists thought it was suspicious that NATO countries began boycotting diplomacy and claim that weapons are the path to peace?

European journalists do not want to report on the polls showing that a vast majority of Ukrainians want immediate negotiations to end the war, as they are committed to the narrative that they are “helping Ukraine” by boycotting diplomacy, deporting Ukrainian refugees to refill the trenches, pushing Zelensky to lower the conscription age, and even pushing for the conscription of women. Political propaganda entails selling war as a selfless and altruistic objective. NATO is not helping Ukraine; NATO has built a proxy army and will fight to the last man. Yulia Tymoshenko, a former Ukrainian presidential candidate and longtime favorite of NATO, stated last year in a response to the head of German intelligence that “what we did not want to believe” has been stated so openly: “At the cost of the very existence of Ukraine and at the cost of the lives of hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians, did someone decide to pay for the ‘weakening’ of Russia for the sake of security in Europe?”

Political leaders think and act in terms of power politics, with the objective to revive the unipolar, hegemonic world order by using Ukrainians to knock Russia out of the ranks of the great powers, so the US can focus its resources on confronting China. Yet, the media consistently sells the war to the public as merely being about “helping” Ukraine.

Fascists as NATO’s Veto Power

The fascist groups in Ukraine are a small minority, yet they have disproportionate power due to how they exercise violence. The Western support for fascists is not the source of a shared ideology, rather it is pragmatism as the fascists are staunchly anti-Russian and highly motivated fighters. Much like the Western support for jihadists in Libya and Syria, the fascists in Ukraine are a means to an end. As Foreign Policy reported in March 2014, shortly after the coup: “The uncomfortable truth is that a sizeable portion of Kiev’s current government—and the protesters who brought it to power—are, indeed, fascists.[12] On 5 February 2022, less than three weeks before the Russian invasion, the leader of fascist organisation C14, Yevhan Karas, argued that the nationalists had been the decisive force at Maidan. Karas recognised that the support from the West was not altruism, rather the West backed them because “we have started a war” that was fulfilling the goals of the West: “we have fun killing and we have fun fighting”.[13]

The nationalists then became a powerful veto power over any efforts by Ukraine to seek peace with Russia. Professor John Mearsheimer accurately argued: “The Americans will side with the Ukrainian right. Because the Americans, and the Ukrainian right, both do not want Zelensky cutting a deal with the Russians that makes it look like the Russians won”.[14] By 2020, the paramilitary constituted about 102,000 men, which was about 40 percent of the entire Ukrainian armed forces.[15]

Ukrainian President Petro Poroshenko went through an astounding transformation from an opponent of Ukrainian nationalism to one of its leading advocates. The BBC reported in August 2015 that a clear majority of 265 MPs out of 450 had supported the first reading of the decentralisation bill to grant more autonomy to Donbas. This sparked a violent veto by the far right, it then reported: “Protesters led by the populist Radical Party and the ultra-nationalist Svoboda (Freedom) party—who oppose any concession to the Russian-backed seperatists” clashed with riot police that resulted in the death of a national guard member and over 100 injured.[16] Poroshenko subsequently began to abandon his efforts to implement the Minsk-2 agreement.

Zelensky was also forced to reverse his position and bow to NATO’s nationalists. Zelensky won the presidential election in April 2019 with the pledge to make peace, running on a peace platform including establishing talks with Donbas, restoring normal relations with Russia, and implementing the Minsk-2 peace agreement. In an astonishing landslide victory of 73 percent of the vote, Zelensky achieved an immense Ukrainian mandate to resolve its conflict with Donbas and Russia. Following his election victory, Zelensky declared his intentions: “I think that we will have personnel changes. In any case we will continue in the direction of the Minsk [peace] talks and head towards concluding a ceasefire”.[17] The nationalists were yet used by NATO as a veto power to prevent peace from breaking out. Rallies against “capitulation” were staged, and Zelensky was rebuked and humiliated by the nationalists when he visited the front to call on pulling back the heavy weapons. Zelensky told the soldiers: “I’m the president of this country. I’m 41 years old. I’m not a loser. I came to you and told you: remove the weapons”.[18] The humiliating encounter was recorded, and the video spread across the internet, revealing that President Zelensky had limited power vis-à-vis the far right as he could do nothing but complain.

The West provided its support to the nationalists by pressuring Zelensky with their government-financed “non-governmental organisations” (NGOs), which have been a key instrument of US intelligence agencies to infiltrate and hijack the civil society of other countries for decades. The most important being the National Endowment for Democracy, established by Reagan and the CIA Director in 1983, The “NGOs” published a long list of red lines, which essentially covered the majority of the peace platform that 73% of Ukrainians had voted for, which even included negotiating with Russia without the participation of the West. Below is the complete list of “red lines”[19]:

Who financed “Ukrainian civil society” that drew a big red line under the peace platform that the vast majority of Ukrainians had voted for? These are the donors[20]:

The simple reality is that Zelensky could not make peace even if he wanted to, as the Western-backed nationalists would march on Kiev if he tried. This is how you engineer a forever war. The Europeans still refuse to make peace without the approval of Ukraine, which now means Zelensky. None other than Boris Johnson recognised how the nationalists limit Zelensky’s power - although Johnson did not mention the relationship between the NATO countries and the nationalists.

To summarise my argument: We will likely never learn exactly what happened at Petropavlivska Borshchahivka due to the central paradox of this proxy war: under the banner of defending Ukraine, the suffering of Ukrainians is concealed, their democratic will is subordinated to geopolitical objectives, and those who expose these contradictions are denounced as enemies of Ukraine.

item.title: Former Head of German Army, General Harald Kujat, Exposes Lies About the Ukraine War
item.description: Harald Kujat, a retired German four-star general, former Chief of Staff of the Bundeswehr and former Chairman of NATO’s Military Committee, argues that the Ukraine war has been prolonged by a series of false Western narratives: that Russia’s invasion was unprovoked, that Moscow intended to conquer all of Ukraine, that Ukraine could achieve military victory, that Russia was unwilling to negotiate, and that continued Western military assistance would eventually change the strategic balance.
item.dc:creator: Glenn Diesen
item.content:encoded:
Harald Kujat, a retired German four-star general, former Chief of Staff of the Bundeswehr and former Chairman of NATO’s Military Committee, argues that the Ukraine war has been prolonged by a series of false Western narratives: that Russia’s invasion was unprovoked, that Moscow intended to conquer all of Ukraine, that Ukraine could achieve military victory, that Russia was unwilling to negotiate, and that continued Western military assistance would eventually change the strategic balance. These assumptions have obstructed diplomatic solutions, contributed to Ukraine’s destruction and brought Europe dangerously close to direct confrontation with Russia. This article outlines arguments made by General Kujat in a podcast last year, with a link below.

The Breakdown of NATO–Russia Relations

Relations between NATO and Russia initially improved substantially after the Cold War. Moscow sought closer cooperation, and mechanisms such as the NATO–Russia Founding Act and NATO–Russia Council established regular political and military dialogue.

Two developments fundamentally damaged this relationship. In 2002, the United States withdrew from the Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty, undermining an essential element of nuclear strategic stability. Russia interpreted the decision as an American attempt to establish strategic superiority.

The second turning point came at NATO’s 2008 Bucharest summit, when Washington pushed for Ukraine and Georgia to become members.

Russia’s two principal strategic objectives have consistently been to avoid military confrontation with the United States and NATO. Moscow therefore sought a security arrangement that would prevent conflicts along its borders from escalating into direct confrontation. NATO’s expansion increasingly concentrated this problem on Ukraine.

The False Narrative of an Unprovoked War

The assertion that Russia’s February 2022 invasion was unprovoked disregards the preceding eight years.

The 2014 overthrow of Ukraine’s democratically elected president, Viktor Yanukovych, was followed by civil war in Eastern Ukraine and severe restrictions on the civil rights of its Russian-speaking population.

The Minsk II agreement of 2015 was intended to resolve this conflict by granting Donbass special constitutional status, protecting Russian language and culture within Ukraine.

Ukraine never implemented these constitutional provisions. Instead, its armed forces were modernised, expanded and rearmed with Western assistance.

Subsequent statements by Angela Merkel and François Hollande indicated that the Minsk process had served to buy time for Ukrainian rearmament rather than resolve the conflict. This constituted a clear act of deception.

In December 2021, Russia proposed security agreements with the United States and NATO. These efforts failed, and the security situation deteriorated into war.

The False Claim That Russia Intended to Conquer Ukraine

Another central misconception is that Russia launched an all-encompassing war to occupy the entire Ukrainian state.

Approximately 170,000 Russian soldiers entered Ukraine against an army of more than 400,000 troops that had received extensive Western training and equipment. The Russian force was insufficient to conquer and occupy the entire country.

The initial objective was more plausibly to overthrow the Ukrainian government and install a pro-Russian leadership, potentially under Viktor Medvedchuk.

When this failed, Russia’s objectives changed. Moscow subsequently sought control of Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson within their former administrative boundaries, alongside a broader security arrangement ensuring Ukraine would not become a platform for NATO military forces.

How the West Undermined the Istanbul Peace Negotiations

The Istanbul negotiations in spring 2022 presented a major opportunity to end the war.

By April 15, both sides had largely negotiated an agreement establishing Ukrainian neutrality and international security guarantees. Outstanding questions concerned the operation of those guarantees and the permitted size and equipment of Ukraine’s armed forces.

These differences were intended to be resolved directly between Presidents Putin and Zelenskyy.

The agreement’s conclusion was torpedoed by Western intervention. Boris Johnson’s April 9 visit to Kiev was particularly consequential, with the British prime minister communicating that Ukraine should continue fighting rather than conclude a settlement.

The strategic objective was subsequently articulated by the American defence secretary: Russia should be weakened politically, economically and militarily.

Ukraine thereby became the battlefield of a proxy war between the United States and Russia, with European governments increasingly assuming responsibility as Washington’s position changed.

The False Promise of Ukrainian Military Victory

Western governments repeatedly maintained that Ukraine could defeat Russia and recover Crimea and the territories in Eastern Ukraine. This was a strategic illusion from the beginning.

Senior military figures recognised the limitations. American General Mark Milley acknowledged that Ukraine had achieved what it could reasonably achieve militarily and should negotiate. Ukrainian commander-in-chief Valery Zaluzhnyi similarly identified enormous equipment requirements that Western countries were unable to fulfil.

Nevertheless, every new weapons system was presented as a potential game-changer. The political formula that Ukraine must not lose and Russia must not win substituted wishful thinking for military strategy.

The consequences were devastating. Opportunities to stop the killing and destruction were repeatedly missed, including Chinese and Brazilian peace initiatives and proposals advanced by German political and security figures.

Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán was harshly criticised for attempting to initiate diplomacy. European governments, meanwhile, made no serious independent effort to negotiate a settlement.

The False Claim That Russia Refuses Negotiations

Russia’s willingness to negotiate has also been misrepresented.

At the June 2025 Istanbul discussions, Moscow submitted a memorandum outlining its proposals for a ceasefire and peace settlement. Ukraine rejected negotiations on that basis, restricting discussions to prisoner exchanges and abducted children.

Russia subsequently insisted that any presidential meeting must be carefully prepared through substantive preliminary negotiations. Ukraine demanded agreement on security guarantees before such a meeting.

These incompatible positions created a diplomatic deadlock, but they did not demonstrate that Russia was unwilling to negotiate.

The Danger of Escalation and Europe’s Strategic Failure

Ukraine’s deteriorating military position has increased the danger of escalation. Attacks against Russia’s nuclear early-warning infrastructure, strategic bomber fleet and other sensitive targets risk expanding the war into a direct confrontation between nuclear powers.

European proposals involving Taurus missiles, NATO troops in Ukraine or a no-fly zone could similarly transform indirect participation into direct military involvement.

The November 2022 missile incident in Poland demonstrated the danger. Former Polish President Andrzej Duda subsequently described pressure from Zelenskyy to attribute the Ukrainian missile to Russia.

European leaders must recognise that expanding the war might prevent Ukraine’s isolated military defeat only at the cost of a potentially catastrophic European conflict.

Europe’s continued commitment to military victory also reflects an unwillingness to acknowledge its earlier strategic mistakes. Rather than supporting American efforts to negotiate, European governments have obstructed them while weakening their own defence capabilities and economies.

Peace Requires a New European Security Order

Military victory and political victory are fundamentally different. Russia has also suffered strategic setbacks, including Finland and Sweden joining NATO and declining Russian influence in the South Caucasus.

Moscow therefore has reasons to seek an end to the war, although its territorial objectives and the question of Ukraine’s neutrality remain central obstacles.

The essential task is not simply achieving a ceasefire. It is establishing a durable European security order that accommodates the interests of Russia and Ukraine, prevents renewed confrontation and restores strategic stability between the nuclear powers.

Europe must abandon the illusion that Russia can be defeated militarily, support serious negotiations and rebuild relations with Washington. Only a negotiated settlement can prevent further Ukrainian destruction and enable Europe to recover its geopolitical influence in an emerging multipolar world.

(This article has been written with the assistance of AI, based on the transcript of the conversation)
